opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think I've ever had a very formal process for it. A lot of it has been driven by taste and by what I find genuinely exciting at a given moment, plus a fairly pragmatic streak.

Early on, when I was doing more hands-on research, I was drawn to problems where I felt the tooling or the infrastructure was the bottleneck. I'd look at something and think, "People aren't making progress here not because the ideas are missing, but because it's painful to try things." That instinct shaped a lot of what I ended up doing. Building tools that let lots of people iterate faster felt like it had more leverage than me personally chasing one more benchmark number.

When it comes to picking a specific research problem, I try to ask a few questions. Is this something where, if it works, it actually changes how people do things, or is it an incremental bump? Do I have some unfair advantage here, whether that's an insight, a dataset, or the engineering ability to try something others find too expensive or annoying? And am I going to stay interested for the year or two it'll take to get anywhere meaningful? If the answer to that last one is no, I've learned it's usually not worth starting.

On methods, I'm pretty empirical. I like to get something running end to end as quickly as possible, even if it's ugly, and then let the experiments tell me where to look. I'm a bit wary of spending too long on elegant theory before you know whether the thing behaves the way you expect in practice. Deep learning in particular has humbled a lot of people who had beautiful arguments for why something should work.

The other thing I'd say is that I pay a lot of attention to the people around me. Some of the best directions I've gotten into came from conversations, from seeing what colleagues were struggling with, or from users of the tools complaining about something. Those complaints are often a really good signal for where the interesting problems are.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say I don't really approach it the way a lot of academics do, where you pick a problem because it's publishable or because it's a gap in the literature. I've always been more driven by friction. I notice something that's annoying, something that gets in the way of me or other people actually doing the work, and I get obsessed with removing that friction.

PyTorch came out of that, honestly. It wasn't "let's go build a deep learning framework." It was that we were trying to do research with Torch7 in Lua, and there was this constant tax on everything. Debugging was painful, the control flow was awkward, you couldn't just drop into the code and poke around the way you'd want to. So the problem chose itself in a sense. The question was never "is this an interesting research direction," it was "why is this so hard, and what would it look like if it weren't."

The other thing I'd say is I try to be honest about taste. A lot of research problems are chosen because they're fashionable, and you can get a lot of mileage out of that, but I find I do my best work when I'm actually curious about the thing, when I'd be happy spending a year on it even if it didn't lead anywhere. So I ask myself whether I'd still want to work on this if nobody cared. If the answer is no, I'm probably not going to do it well.

On methods, I'm pretty pragmatic. I'll use whatever gets me to an answer fastest, and I try not to be ideological about tools or techniques. That sounds obvious, but there's a lot of tribalism in this field, and I think it holds people back. The method should serve the question, not the other way around. And I like methods where I can see what's going on, where the system is legible to me. If I can't inspect it and build intuition about why it works, I don't trust it, and I don't enjoy working with it.

And I think the last piece is that I care a lot about who's going to use the thing. Research that lives in a paper and never touches anyone's workflow is fine, there's a place for it, but I'm more motivated when I can picture the person on the other end, the grad student at two in the morning trying to get a model to train. If I'm making their life better, that's the signal I'm looking for.

r002.rationale: It says he will use whatever method gets to an answer fastest, avoids being ideological about tools, and treats the method as serving the question.

astra-6.text:
For me, it starts with an intuition about something that should be possible, or something that feels unnecessarily difficult. Then I try to make that intuition concrete: what’s the actual question, and what experiment would tell me whether there’s anything there?

I tend to work backward from the problem rather than start with a method I want to use. It’s easy to become attached to a particular technique and keep finding places to apply it. I’d rather ask what the simplest approach is that could teach us something, try that, and let the result change my thinking.

There’s also a personal component: am I curious enough about this to stay with it when the first few ideas don’t work? You need that, because choosing a problem is only the beginning. A lot of research is figuring out whether a failure means your approach is wrong, your experiment is wrong, or the question itself needs to change.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to start with something that bothers me—something we ought to be able to do, but that feels unnecessarily difficult. Then I try to understand whether the limitation is in our ideas, our tools, or just an assumption that everyone has stopped questioning.

For methods, I like starting with the simplest experiment that could teach me something. You can spend a lot of time building an elaborate system before finding out that the underlying intuition was wrong. I’d rather get that feedback early, change my mind, and keep going.

And I think personal interest matters. Research involves spending a long time being confused. If you choose a problem only because it’s fashionable, it’s harder to stay with it when the obvious approaches stop working.
